Monomial ideals with tiny squares

Shalom Eliahou, Jürgen Herzog and Maryam Mohammadi Saem Address: Shalom Eliahou, Univ. Littoral Côte d’Opale, EA 2597 - LMPA - Laboratoire de Mathématiques Pures et Appliquées Joseph Liouville, F-62228 Calais, France and CNRS, FR 2956, France Email address: eliahou@univ-littoral.fr Address: Jürgen Herzog, Fachbereich Mathematik, Universität Duisburg-Essen, Campus Essen, 45117 Essen, Germany Email address: juergen.herzog@uni-essen.de Address: Maryam Mohammadi Saem, Faculty of Science, University of Mohaghegh Ardabili, P.O. Box 179, Ardabil, Iran Email address: m.mohammadisaem@yahoo.com
Abstract.

Let I⊂K⁡[x,y]I\subset K[x,y] be a monomial ideal. How small can μ⁡(I2)\mu(I^{2}) be in terms of μ⁡(I)\mu(I)? It has been expected that the inequality μ⁡(I2)>μ⁡(I)\mu(I^{2})>\mu(I) should hold whenever μ⁡(I)≥2\mu(I)\geq 2. Here we disprove this expectation and provide a somewhat surprising answer to the above question.

1. Introduction

For an ideal II in a Noetherian ring RR, let μ⁡(I)\mu(I) denote as usual the least number of generators of II. If μ⁡(I)=m\mu(I)=m, how small can μ⁡(I2)\mu(I^{2}) be in terms of mm? Obviously, in suitable rings with zero-divisors, we may have μ⁡(I2)=0\mu(I^{2})=0. There even exist one-dimensional local domains (R,𝔪)(R,{\mathfrak{m}}) with the property that the square of their maximal ideal 𝔪{\mathfrak{m}} requires less generators than 𝔪{\mathfrak{m}} itself, see [1, 2]. However, if RR is a regular local ring, or if RR is a polynomial ring over a field KK and II is a homogeneous ideal of RR, it has been expected in [3] that the inequality μ⁡(I2)>μ⁡(I)\mu(I^{2})>\mu(I) should hold whenever μ⁡(I)≥2\mu(I)\geq 2. This is indeed the case for any integrally closed ideal II in a 22-dimensional regular local ring. On the other hand, it is not too difficult to construct examples of monomial ideals II in a polynomial ring SS with at least 4 variables such that μ⁡(I2)<μ⁡(I)\mu(I^{2})<\mu(I). However, these examples satisfy height⁡I<dimS\operatorname{height}I<\dim S. So far no ideals II with μ⁡(I2)<μ⁡(I)\mu(I^{2})<\mu(I) were known for 22-dimensional regular rings. In this paper, we shall prove the following statements.

Theorem 1.1.

For every integer m≥5m\geq 5, there exists a monomial ideal I⊂K⁡[x,y]I\subset K[x,y] such that μ⁡(I)=m\mu(I)=m and μ⁡(I2)=9\mu(I^{2})=9.

Moreover, this result is best possible for m≥6m\geq 6.

Theorem 1.2.

Let I⊂K⁡[x,y]I\subset K[x,y] be a monomial ideal. If μ⁡(I)≥6\mu(I)\geq 6 then μ⁡(I2)≥9\mu(I^{2})\geq 9.

Here are some notation to be used throughout. We denote by ℳ\mathcal{M} the set of monomials in K⁡[x,y]K[x,y], i.e.

ℳ={xiyj∣i,j∈ℕ}.\mathcal{M}=\{x^{i}y^{j}\mid i,j\in{\mathbb{N}}\}.

As usual, we view ℳ\mathcal{M} as partially ordered by divisibility.

For a monomial ideal J⊂K⁡[x,y]J\subset K[x,y], we denote by 𝒢⁡(J)\mathcal{G}(J) its unique minimal system of monomial generators. It is well known that 𝒢⁡(J)\mathcal{G}(J) is of cardinality μ⁡(J)\mu(J) and consists of all monomials in JJ which are minimal under divisibility, i.e.

𝒢⁡(J)=(ℳ∩J)∖(ℳ∩J)​ℳ∗\mathcal{G}(J)=\big(\mathcal{M}\cap J\big)\setminus\big(\mathcal{M}\cap J\big)\mathcal{M}^{*}

where ℳ∗=ℳ∖{1}\mathcal{M}^{*}=\mathcal{M}\setminus\{1\}.

Finally, given integers a≤ba\leq b, we denote by [a,b][a,b] the integer interval they span, i.e.

[a,b]={c∈ℤ∣a≤c≤b}.[a,b]=\{c\in{\mathbb{Z}}\mid a\leq c\leq b\}.

2. Preliminaries

Let m≥2m\geq 2 be an integer and let I⊂K⁡[x,y]I\subset K[x,y] be a monomial ideal such that μ⁡(I)=m\mu(I)=m. Then 𝒢⁡(I)={u1,…,um}\mathcal{G}(I)=\{u_{1},\dots,u_{m}\}, where ui=xai​ybiu_{i}=x^{a_{i}}y^{b_{i}} for all ii and where the exponents ai,bi∈ℕa_{i},b_{i}\in{\mathbb{N}} satisfy

(1) a1>a2>⋯>am,b1<b2<⋯<bm.\begin{array}[]{lcr}&a_{1}>a_{2}>\dots>a_{m},&\\ &b_{1}<b_{2}<\dots<b_{m}.&\end{array}

Removing any common factor among the uiu_{i}, we may assume am=b1=0a_{m}=b_{1}=0 if desired.

Let V={(i,j)∈ℕ2∣1≤i≤j≤m}V=\{(i,j)\in{\mathbb{N}}^{2}\mid 1\leq i\leq j\leq m\}, and consider the map

f:V→I2(i,j)↦ui​uj.\begin{array}[]{rccc}f\colon&V&\rightarrow&I^{2}\\ &(i,j)&\mapsto&u_{i}u_{j}.\end{array}

Then f⁡(V)f(V) generates I2I^{2}, but not minimally so in general. Thus 𝒢⁡(I2)⊆f⁡(V)\mathcal{G}(I^{2})\subseteq f(V), with equality only occurring in special circumstances. How small can 𝒢⁡(I2)\mathcal{G}(I^{2}) be? So far this was not well understood. We provide a complete answer in this note.

We partially order ℕ2{\mathbb{N}}^{2} as follows:

(i,j)≤(k,l)⟺i≤k​ and ​j≤l.(i,j)\leq(k,l)\Longleftrightarrow i\leq k\mbox{ and }j\leq l.

Since V⊂ℕ2V\subset{\mathbb{N}}^{2}, we also view VV as partially ordered by ≤\leq. Recall that ℳ\mathcal{M} is partially ordered by divisibility. These orderings interact in a simple yet useful way, as shown by the lemma below. Recall that an antichain in a poset is a subset whose elements are pairwise noncomparable.

Lemma 2.1.

Let v,v′∈Vv,v^{\prime}\in V. If f⁡(v)f(v) divides f⁡(v′)f(v^{\prime}), then either v=v′v=v^{\prime} or else {v,v′}\{v,v^{\prime}\} is an antichain in VV.

Equivalently, if v<v′v<v^{\prime}, then {f⁡(v),f⁡(v′)}\{f(v),f(v^{\prime})\} is an antichain in ℳ\mathcal{M}.

Proof.

Set v=(i,j),v′=(k,l)v=(i,j),\,v^{\prime}=(k,l), and assume v<v′v<v^{\prime}. Then i≤ki\leq k and j≤lj\leq l, and at least one of these inequalities is strict. We have f⁡(v)=ui​uj=xai+aj​ybi+bjf(v)=u_{i}u_{j}=x^{a_{i}+a_{j}}y^{b_{i}+b_{j}}. Similarly, f⁡(v′)=xak+al​ybk+blf(v^{\prime})=x^{a_{k}+a_{l}}y^{b_{k}+b_{l}}. Since the ata_{t} are decreasing and the btb_{t} are increasing, and since either i<ki<k or j<lj<l, we have

ai+aj\displaystyle a_{i}+a_{j} >\displaystyle> ak+bl,\displaystyle a_{k}+b_{l},
bi+bj\displaystyle b_{i}+b_{j} <\displaystyle< bk+bl.\displaystyle b_{k}+b_{l}.

Therefore, neither ui​uju_{i}u_{j} divides uk​ulu_{k}u_{l}, nor conversely.    ∎

Remark 2.2.

If v,v′∈Vv,v^{\prime}\in V, then v,v′v,v^{\prime} are noncomparable if and only if

min⁡v<min⁡v′≤max⁡v′<max⁡v​ or ​min​v′<min⁡v≤max⁡v<max⁡v′.\min v<\min v^{\prime}\leq\max v^{\prime}<\max v\,\,\textrm{ or }\,\,\min v^{\prime}<\min v\leq\max v<\max v^{\prime}.

Picturing any pair w=(i,j)∈Vw=(i,j)\in V as an edge joining the vertices i,j∈ℕi,j\in{\mathbb{N}}, it is useful to keep in mind that graphically, noncomparable pairs v,v′∈Vv,v^{\prime}\in V look like this:

For instance, if v=(1,3)v=(1,3), the only element of VV which is noncomparable to vv is v′=(2,2)v^{\prime}=(2,2), as is graphically obvious. Therefore by Lemma 2.1, if u1​u3∉𝒢⁡(I2)u_{1}u_{3}\notin\mathcal{G}(I^{2}), then the only element of 𝒢⁡(I2)\mathcal{G}(I^{2}) dividing u1​u3u_{1}u_{3} must be u22u_{2}^{2}.

Of course, noncomparability is not a transitive relation. For instance, the only elements of VV which are noncomparable to v′=(2,2)v^{\prime}=(2,2) are all v′′∈Vv^{\prime\prime}\in V of the form v′′=(1,j)v^{\prime\prime}=(1,j) with j∈[3,m]j\in[3,m]. We shall also need the next lemma.

Lemma 2.3.

Let v,v1,v2∈Vv,v_{1},v_{2}\in V. Assume that v1≤v2v_{1}\leq v_{2} and that f⁡(v)f(v) divides both f⁡(v1),f⁡(v2)f(v_{1}),f(v_{2}). Then f⁡(v)f(v) divides f⁡(v′)f(v^{\prime}) for all v′∈Vv^{\prime}\in V such that v1≤v′≤v2v_{1}\leq v^{\prime}\leq v_{2}.

Proof.

Set v=(i,j),v1=(i1,j1),v2=(i2,j2),v′=(r,s)v=(i,j),v_{1}=(i_{1},j_{1}),v_{2}=(i_{2},j_{2}),v^{\prime}=(r,s). The hypotheses, together with the respective monotonicity of the ata_{t} and btb_{t}, imply

ai+aj\displaystyle a_{i}+a_{j} ≤\displaystyle\leq ai2+aj2,\displaystyle a_{i_{2}}+a_{j_{2}},
bi+bj\displaystyle b_{i}+b_{j} ≤\displaystyle\leq bi1+bj1.\displaystyle b_{i_{1}}+b_{j_{1}}.

Since i1≤r≤i2i_{1}\leq r\leq i_{2} and j1≤s≤j2j_{1}\leq s\leq j_{2}, it follows that

bi1+bj1\displaystyle b_{i_{1}}+b_{j_{1}} ≤\displaystyle\leq br+bs.\displaystyle b_{r}+b_{s}.

Thus ai+aj≤ar+asa_{i}+a_{j}\leq a_{r}+a_{s} and bi+bj≤br+bsb_{i}+b_{j}\leq b_{r}+b_{s}, whence f⁡(v)f(v) divides f⁡(v′)f(v^{\prime}).    ∎

3. Conditions for tiny squares

We now give conditions on a monomial ideal I=(u1,…,um)I=(u_{1},\dots,u_{m}) in K⁡[x,y]K[x,y] which will force μ⁡(I2)\mu(I^{2}) to be a small constant.

Theorem 3.1.

Let m≥5m\geq 5. Let I=(u1,…,um)⊂K⁡[x,y]I=(u_{1},\dots,u_{m})\subset K[x,y] be a monomial ideal with ui=xai​ybiu_{i}=x^{a_{i}}y^{b_{i}} for all ii, where a1>⋯>ama_{1}>\dots>a_{m} and b1<⋯<bmb_{1}<\dots<b_{m}. Assume that the following divisibility conditions hold:

(2) u1​um\displaystyle u_{1}u_{m} |\displaystyle| u2​um−1\displaystyle u_{2}u_{m-1}
(3) u1​um−1\displaystyle u_{1}u_{m-1} |\displaystyle| u2​u3,um−22\displaystyle u_{2}u_{3},\,u_{m-2}^{2}
(4) u22\displaystyle u_{2}^{2} |\displaystyle| u1​u3,u1​um−2\displaystyle u_{1}u_{3},\,u_{1}u_{m-2}
(5) u2​um\displaystyle u_{2}u_{m} |\displaystyle| u3​um−1,um−2​um−1\displaystyle u_{3}u_{m-1},\,u_{m-2}u_{m-1}
(6) um−12\displaystyle u_{m-1}^{2} |\displaystyle| u3​um,um−2​um.\displaystyle u_{3}u_{m},\,u_{m-2}u_{m}.

Then μ⁡(I2)=9\mu(I^{2})=9. More precisely, I2I^{2} is minimally generated by the set

G={u12,u1​u2,u22}∪{u1​um−1,u1​um,u2​um}∪{um−12,um−1​um,um2}.G=\{u_{1}^{2},u_{1}u_{2},u_{2}^{2}\}\cup\{u_{1}u_{m-1},u_{1}u_{m},u_{2}u_{m}\}\cup\{u_{m-1}^{2},u_{m-1}u_{m},u_{m}^{2}\}.
Proof.

To see that GG generates I2I^{2}, we must show that, for all i,j∈[1,m]i,j\in[1,m] such that i≤ji\leq j, the monomial ui​uju_{i}u_{j} is a multiple of some element in GG . We distinguish several cases.

Case i=1.i=1. If j∈{1,2,m−1,m}j\in\{1,2,m-1,m\}, we are done since the corresponding monomial u1​uju_{1}u_{j} belongs to GG. Assume now j∈[3,m−2]j\in[3,m-2]. Then (1,3)≤(1,j)≤(1,m−2)(1,3)\leq(1,j)\leq(1,m-2), and since u22u_{2}^{2} divides both u1​u3u_{1}u_{3} and u1​um−2u_{1}u_{m-2} by (4), it also divides u1​uju_{1}u_{j} by Lemma 2.3.

Case i,j∈[2,m−2].i,j\in[2,m-2]. If (i,j)=(2,2)(i,j)=(2,2), we are done since u22∈Gu_{2}^{2}\in G. Case j=m−1j=m-1. If i=2i=2, then by (2), u2​um−1u_{2}u_{m-1} is divisible by u1​umu_{1}u_{m} and u1​um∈Gu_{1}u_{m}\in G. If i∈[3,m−2]i\in[3,m-2], then (3,m−1)≤(i,m−1)≤(m−2,m−1)(3,m-1)\leq(i,m-1)\leq(m-2,m-1), and since u2​umu_{2}u_{m} divides both u3​um−1u_{3}u_{m-1} and um−2​um−1u_{m-2}u_{m-1} by (5), it also divides ui​um−1u_{i}u_{m-1} by Lemma 2.3. Finally, if i=m−1i=m-1, we are done since um−12∈Gu_{m-1}^{2}\in G.

If i∈[3,m−2]i\in[3,m-2], then (3,m)≤(i,m)≤(m−2,m)(3,m)\leq(i,m)\leq(m-2,m), and since um−12u_{m-1}^{2} divides both u3​umu_{3}u_{m} and um−2​umu_{m-2}u_{m} by (6), it also divides ui​umu_{i}u_{m} by Lemma 2.3. Finally, if i∈{m−1,m}i\in\{m-1,m\}, we are done since um−1​um,um2∈Gu_{m-1}u_{m},u_{m}^{2}\in G.

We conclude that GG generates I2I^{2}. To establish the equality G=𝒢⁡(I2)G=\mathcal{G}(I^{2}), it remains to see that GG is an antichain. Let A⊂VA\subset V consist of nine pairs (i,j)(i,j) such that G={ui​uj∣(i,j)∈A}G=\{u_{i}u_{j}\mid(i,j)\in A\}, for instance

A={(1,1),(1,2),(2,2),(1,m−1),(1,m),(2,m),(m−1,m−1),(m−1,m),(m,m)}.A=\{(1,1),(1,2),(2,2),(1,m-1),(1,m),(2,m),(m-1,m-1),(m-1,m),(m,m)\}.

Replacing (2,2)(2,2) by (1,3)(1,3) and (m−1,m−1)(m-1,m-1) by (m−2,m)(m-2,m) yields a chain in VV, namely

(1,1)<(1,2)<(1,3)<\displaystyle(1,1)<(1,2)<(1,3)<
(1,m−1)<(1,m)<(2,m)<\displaystyle(1,m-1)<(1,m)<(2,m)<

G′=G∪{u1​u3,um−2​um}∖{u22,um−12}G^{\prime}=G\cup\{u_{1}u_{3},u_{m-2}u_{m}\}\setminus\{u_{2}^{2},u_{m-1}^{2}\}

Since GG generates I2I^{2}, then u1​u3u_{1}u_{3} is a multiple of some element of GG. Moreover, since G′G^{\prime} is an antichain, the only possible factors of u1​u3u_{1}u_{3} in GG are u22u_{2}^{2} and um−12u_{m-1}^{2}. But since (1,3)<(m−1,m−1)(1,3)<(m-1,m-1), Lemma 2.1 implies that {u1​u3,um−12}\{u_{1}u_{3},u_{m-1}^{2}\} is an antichain. Therefore, the only factor of u1​u3u_{1}u_{3} in GG is u22u_{2}^{2}. Hence, since any monomial in I2I^{2} has at least one factor in G∩𝒢⁡(I2)G\cap\mathcal{G}(I^{2}), it follows that u22∈𝒢⁡(I2)u_{2}^{2}\in\mathcal{G}(I^{2}).

But neither possibility arises, since u1​um−1u_{1}u_{m-1} divides u2​u3u_{2}u_{3} by (3), and u1​umu_{1}u_{m} divides u2​um−1u_{2}u_{m-1} by (2).

Entirely symmetric arguments apply to um−12u_{m-1}^{2}. We conclude that G=𝒢⁡(I2)G=\mathcal{G}(I^{2}), as desired.    ∎

4. An explicit construction

We now show that the conditions of Theorem 3.1 ensuring μ⁡(I2)=9\mu(I^{2})=9 are realizable.

Proposition 4.1.

Let m≥5m\geq 5. Let I=(u1,…,um)I=(u_{1},\dots,u_{m}), where ui=xai​ybiu_{i}=x^{a_{i}}y^{b_{i}} with exponents ai,bia_{i},b_{i} defined as follows:

(a1,…,am)\displaystyle(a_{1},\dots,a_{m}) =\displaystyle= (5​m,4​m,4​m−1,…,3​m+4,m,0),\displaystyle(5m,4m,4m-1,\dots,3m+4,m,0),
(b1,…,bm)\displaystyle(b_{1},\dots,b_{m}) =\displaystyle= (am,…,a1).\displaystyle(a_{m},\dots,a_{1}).

Then μ⁡(I)=m\mu(I)=m and μ⁡(I2)=9\mu(I^{2})=9.

Proof.

Since the aia_{i} are decreasing and the bib_{i} are increasing, the uiu_{i} constitute an antichain and hence a minimal system of generators of II. In order to show μ⁡(I2)=9\mu(I^{2})=9, it suffices to prove that the divisibility conditions of Theorem 3.1 are met. This is straightforward. For convenience, here are the monomials involved:

u1​um=x5​m​y5​mu2​um−1=x5​m​y5​mu1​um−1=x6​m​y4​mu2​u3=x8​m−1​y4​m+4um−22=x6​m+8​y8​m−2u22=x8​m​y2​mu1​u3=x9​m−1​y3​m+4u1​um−2=x8​m+4​y4​m−1u2​um=x4​m​y6​mu3​um−1=x5​m−1​y7​m+4um−2​um−1=x4​m+4​y8​m−1um−12=x2​m​y8​mu3​um=x4​m−1​y8​m+4um−2​um=x3​m+4​y9​m−1.\begin{array}[]{lll}u_{1}u_{m}=x^{5m}y^{5m}&u_{2}u_{m-1}=x^{5m}y^{5m}&\\ u_{1}u_{m-1}=x^{6m}y^{4m}&u_{2}u_{3}=x^{8m-1}y^{4m+4}&u_{m-2}^{2}=x^{6m+8}y^{8m-2}\\ u_{2}^{2}=x^{8m}y^{2m}&u_{1}u_{3}=x^{9m-1}y^{3m+4}&u_{1}u_{m-2}=x^{8m+4}y^{4m-1}\\ u_{2}u_{m}=x^{4m}y^{6m}&u_{3}u_{m-1}=x^{5m-1}y^{7m+4}&u_{m-2}u_{m-1}=x^{4m+4}y^{8m-1}\\ u_{m-1}^{2}=x^{2m}y^{8m}&u_{3}u_{m}=x^{4m-1}y^{8m+4}&u_{m-2}u_{m}=x^{3m+4}y^{9m-1}.\end{array}

Let us now look at the degree distribution of 𝒢⁡(I)\mathcal{G}(I) and of 𝒢⁡(I2)\mathcal{G}(I^{2}). The generators uiu_{i} of II are of degree ai+bi=ai+am+1−ia_{i}+b_{i}=a_{i}+a_{m+1-i} for all i∈[1,m]i\in[1,m]. For m≥5m\geq 5, we find

deg⁡(u1)=deg⁡(u2)=deg⁡(um−1)=deg⁡(um)=5​m,deg⁡(ui)=deg⁡(um+1−i)=7​m+3\begin{array}[]{rcl}\deg(u_{1})=\deg(u_{2})=\deg(u_{m-1})=\deg(u_{m})&=&5m,\\ \deg(u_{i})=\deg(u_{m+1-i})&=&7m+3\end{array}

for all 3≤i≤m−23\leq i\leq m-2. That is, the ideal II is generated in two degrees only. For I2I^{2} the situation is even simpler. It is generated in the single degree 10​m10m, the common degree of its nine minimal generators.

Example 4.2.

Here is the case m=10m=10 of Proposition 4.1. We have

I=(x50,x40​y10,x39​y34,x38​y35,x37​y36,x36​y37,x35​y38,x34​y39,x10​y40,y50)I=(x^{50},\,x^{40}y^{10},\,x^{39}y^{34},\,x^{38}y^{35},\,x^{37}y^{36},\,x^{36}y^{37},\,x^{35}y^{38},\,x^{34}y^{39},\,x^{10}y^{40},\,y^{50})

and

I2=(x100,x90​y10,x80​y20,x60​y40,x50​y50,x40​y60,x20​y80,x10​y90,y100).I^{2}=(x^{100},\,x^{90}y^{10},\,x^{80}y^{20},\,x^{60}y^{40},\,x^{50}y^{50},\,x^{40}y^{60},\,x^{20}y^{80},\,x^{10}y^{90},\,y^{100}).

To conclude this section, let us show that in contrast, if II is generated in a single degree, then μ⁡(I2)\mu(I^{2}) grows to infinity with μ⁡(I)\mu(I).

Proposition 4.3.

Let I⊂K⁡[x,y]I\subset K[x,y] be a monomial ideal generated in a single degree. If μ⁡(I)=m\mu(I)=m then μ⁡(I2)≥2​m−1\mu(I^{2})\geq 2m-1.

Proof.

Set 𝒢⁡(I)={u1,…,um}\mathcal{G}(I)=\{u_{1},\dots,u_{m}\}, and assume deg⁡(ui)=d\deg(u_{i})=d for all ii. Since deg⁡(ui​uj)=2​d\deg(u_{i}u_{j})=2d for all i,ji,j, the distinct ui​uju_{i}u_{j} form an antichain for divisibility. Hence μ⁡(I2)\mu(I^{2}) equals the number of pairwise distinct ui​uju_{i}u_{j}. Now that number is at least 2​m−12m-1, as witnessed by the subset

u1​um\displaystyle u_{1}u_{m} |\displaystyle| u2​um−1,\displaystyle u_{2}u_{m-1},

and we would be done. Assume for a contradiction the contrary, i.e. that γ⁡(u1​um−1)=γ⁡(u2​um)\gamma(u_{1}u_{m-1})=\gamma(u_{2}u_{m}). Lemma 6.1 then implies

Thus ur​us∈A′u_{r}u_{s}\in A^{\prime}, contrary to the conjunction of (17) and (15). This contradiction settles (16) and concludes the proof of the present last case, and hence of the theorem.    ∎

For completeness, let us give optimal lower bounds on μ⁡(I2)\mu(I^{2}) for monomial ideals I⊂K⁡[x,y]I\subset K[x,y] such that μ⁡(I)=m≤5\mu(I)=m\leq 5. The result is as follows.

μ⁡(I2)≥{1 if ​m=1,3 if ​m=2,5 if ​m=3,7 if ​m=4,8 if ​m=5.\mu(I^{2})\geq\left\{\begin{array}[]{cc}1&\textrm{ if }m=1,\\ 3&\textrm{ if }m=2,\\ 5&\textrm{ if }m=3,\\ 7&\textrm{ if }m=4,\\ 8&\textrm{ if }m=5.\end{array}\right.

As stated, these five lower bounds are sharp. The verification is left to the reader.

Let us conclude this paper with two questions. Let m≥6m\geq 6 be an integer, and let I⊂K⁡[x,y]I\subset K[x,y] be a monomial ideal such that μ⁡(I)=m\mu(I)=m. We have seen in Proposition 4.3 that if II is generated in a single degree, then μ⁡(I2)≥2​m−1\mu(I^{2})\geq 2m-1. Our ideals in Proposition 4.1 reaching the absolute minimum μ⁡(I2)=9\mu(I^{2})=9 are generated in two degrees depending on mm, namely 5​m5m and 7​m+37m+3.

Here is our first question. If II is generated in two degrees d1<d2d_{1}<d_{2} such that the difference d=d2−d1d=d_{2}-d_{1} is fixed and independent of mm, does it follow that μ⁡(I2)\mu(I^{2}) must grow to infinity with mm? This seems to be true for d=1d=1, but it would be nice to have a proof.

Our second question is, what would be the proper generalization of the present results in nn variables?
